content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a new backdoor attack that aims to insert an architecture component to make the model have a wrong prediction on the triggered example while maintain a good performance on normal inputs. Specifically, it introduce a special activation function called MaliciousAdaptiveAvgPool that first detect the existence of the trigger and then uses a min-pooling to combine the result. To further improve the performance, it uses the combination of average pooling on the white-pixel and black-pixel to make the activation focus on the trigger region. Experiment results on normal, fine-tuning and trained from scratch settings show the effectiveness of the proposed method. It could maintain a relatively high clean accuracy on normal example and achieve a random guess on triggered example. It has also tried to use neural architecture search to find a better architecture component however it does not work.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
1. The proposed setting is quite interesting and novel. 
2. The experiment results shows the proposed method could maintain a high clean accuracy on normal example and achieve a random guess on triggered example, which proves the effectiveness of the proposed method.


Cons:
1. Although the proposed method want to build a stronger backdoor, it is limited by a lot of other aspects like the trigger design and the significant difference between trigger and clean examples. For example, if the dataset is a black and white dataset such as MNIST, the proposed method will not work. Or the trigger now is not a square but a specific noise like Blended attack or invisible trigger attack. And it is no easy task to adapt the proposed method as well. The pooling has to be constructed very carefully. 
2. Because of the reasons in Cons 1, I think the proposed method won't work in setting 2 and 3 if the datasets used for fine-tuning and retraining has some overlap with the trigger. For example, the proposed method would work when the trigger is white and the data's background is white as well. 
3. The proposed method could only work in untargeted setting which limits its significance as the previous backdoor could do both targeted and untargeted settings.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is in general clear. However, I still find some notations not defined. For example,  the (a) (c) is not defined in the  "Our ‘malicious’ activation function is composed of the following steps:" part. It should be step 1 and 3 if I understand it correctly. It would be better to separate the trigger detection part and activation poisoning part.

Quality: The paper is well-written and the experiment is OK to me.

Novelty: The proposed setting is novel and quite interesting. Although the proposed method could only handle some easy settings, it has a good potential to make it stronger in future works.

Reproducibility: The training hyper-parameter is not provided so it is hard to judge whether it is reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a new and novel backdoor attack that inserts some architecture component to make the model have a wrong prediction on the triggered example. However, the proposed method is heavily restricted by the trigger design and used datasets.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new backdoor attack on neural networks. Contrary to the existing literature where the backdoors are planted to the model weights through training, the authors propose manipulating the model architecture so that it naturally would have a backdoor. The motivation behind this method, called Model Architecture Backdoor (MAB), is that if backdoored model weights are re-adjusted, the backdoors might be erased. However, suppose the model architecture inherently allows backdoors. In that case, the attacker can achieve its goal no matter what the weights are. To materialize this idea, the paper proposes to create a shortcut from the inputs to the output that can activate the activations of the penultimate layer of a neural network and design this process deterministically. Experimental results over several standard image datasets show that the proposed method can pose threats against neural networks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths:
- The general idea of the paper is novel and exciting. Having model architectures that naturally allow backdoors can pose a significant threat to neural networks. The proposed line of work can be thought-provoking.

### Weaknesses:
- While the paper's general idea is interesting, the authors need to present a systematic framework for constructing such architectural attacks. Instead, the paper intuitively goes over a particular attack design without proper motivation and reasoning. A more systematic approach for planting such backdoors is needed so that one can apply them to different models. The proposed method seems like a case study for AlexNet vulnerabilities at this stage.

- The writing of the paper up to the proposed method seems fine. However, after that point, many gray areas leave the readers wondering. For instance:

   1. Why steps 1-4 are taken to find a backdoor? Are there any other alternatives? How the hyper-parameters $\beta, \alpha,$ and $\delta$ are selected? Why can these hyper-parameters not raise suspicion from users? 

   2. During the proposed method, the paper discusses the MAB for AlexNet as if the proposed method is only valid for this architecture. However, in the experimental results, the paper suddenly switches to VGG-11. To which models can MAB be applied? For instance, can one use it for ResNets?

3. What is the motivation behind discussions of Sec. 5.1? I recommend adding a few connecting sentences between this section and the previous one to set the tone and explain the goal of the material presented in Sec. 5.1.

- The experimental results are limited. First, more advanced backdoor attacks such as Refool [1] or WaNet [2] have been proposed. Second, the performance of the trained models in terms of clean accuracy is worse than the current SOTA. Finally, no attempts to test the model with existing backdoor detection algorithms such as [3] that consider the topology of the neurons have been made. These extra experiments are essential for the paper to be convincing.

[1] Liu, Yunfei, et al. "Reflection backdoor: A natural backdoor attack on deep neural networks." *ECCV*, 2020.

[2] Nguyen, Anh, and Anh Tran. "WaNet--Imperceptible Warping-based Backdoor Attack." *ICLR*, 2021.

[3] Zheng et al. "Topological detection of Trojaned neural networks," NeurIPS, 2021.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Detailed comments are given in the **Strength And Weaknesses**. Below is a summary:

#### **Clarity**: Some sections in the paper (please see above) lack enough clarity, which makes the article difficult to understand.

#### **Quality**: The paper needs a better presentation and a more systematic framework for it to be considered of high quality. At this stage, it is solely a novel idea.

#### **Novelty And Reproducibility**: The paper's idea seems extremely exciting in terms of novelty. However, the execution of the concept needs to be cooked up. The authors claim in the supplement that they will provide the code base to help with reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: Based on the abovementioned concerns, I vote for the rejection of this paper at this stage.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a new form of backdoor attacks called architectural backdoor. Architectural backdoors modifies the network architecture to inject the backdoor. Specifically, the authors add an extra residual path from the input image to the features at average pooling layer. This extra layer/path will detect if the trigger is present and if so will modify the feature embedding.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
1. The paper is well-written and the idea is easy to understand.
2. The idea is interesting. The paper explored a new way to inject backdoor: by modifying the network architectures directly.


Weaknesses:
1. In general, any backdoor attack method should be general to the actual trigger they use. In seems that the proposed backdoor injection method can only handle the white box backdoor and checkerboard backdoor. How would your approach be applicable to other patch pattern. 
2. The proposed architectural backdoor seems to be not actually modifying the network architecture. It is simply adding an extra path between the input and the feature embedding. This is not surprising as it is expected that the model will behave differently since you are modifying the representations directly. In practice, such an approach is easy to detect, by simply checking the implemented model architecture. 
3. It seems that the proposed architecture backdoor does not involve any learnable parameters. Then it is not surprising that the proposed attack is able to survive retraining or fine-tuning. I wonder if an attack is possible by modifying the architecture directly, for example, kernel sizes or replacing avgpooling with maxpooling.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: This paper is written clearly. 
Quality: The quality is good.
Novelty: Limited novelty.
Reproducibility: The authors have not provide their code.
content.summary_of_the_review: I find the idea proposed in this paper is interesting. However, the idea seems very simple and it is not surprising that the proposed backdoor is effective. What’s more, I feel that this is not really “architecture backdoor” as it is very easy to detect since it is simply adding an extra path between the input and the feature embedding. Thus i am recommending reject.

content.title: Architectural Backdoors in Neural Networks
content.abstract: Machine learning is vulnerable to adversarial manipulation. Previous literature has demonstrated that at the training stage attackers can manipulate data (Gu et al.) and data sampling procedures (Shumailov et al.) to control model behaviour. A common attack goal is to plant backdoors i.e. force the victim model to learn to recognise a trigger known only by the adversary. In this paper, we introduce a new class of backdoor attacks that hide inside  model architectures i.e. in the inductive bias of the functions used to train. These backdoors are simple to implement, for instance by publishing open-source code for a backdoored model architecture that others will reuse unknowingly. We demonstrate that model architectural backdoors represent a real threat and, unlike other approaches, can survive a complete re-training from scratch. We formalise the main construction principles behind architectural backdoors, such as a link between the input and the output, and describe some possible protections against them. We evaluate our attacks on computer vision benchmarks of different scales and demonstrate the underlying vulnerability is pervasive in a variety of common training settings.
